title: 10 — Key Vault, App Configuration & Secrets
html:
10 — Key Vault, App Configuration & Secrets

Key Vault stores the things that must stay secret. App Configuration stores the things that must change without a redeploy. They're complementary, and most teams use only the first.

1. Key Vault: three object types

Object Stores Use
Secret Any string ≤ 25 KB Connection strings, API keys, passwords, tokens
Key An asymmetric or symmetric key — the private material never leaves the vault Signing, encryption, customer-managed keys, HSM-backed operations
Certificate An X.509 cert + its private key, with lifecycle management TLS certificates, with auto-renewal from an integrated CA

The distinction that matters for keys: you don't retrieve a key — you send data to the vault and it performs the sign/encrypt operation. The private material is never exposed, which is the whole point (and why key operations are slower and rate-limited).

Tiers: Standard (software-protected) and Premium (HSM-backed, FIPS 140-2 Level 2). Managed HSM is a separate, single-tenant, Level 3 service for strict regulatory requirements at much higher cost.

2. Access control: RBAC, not access policies

resource vault 'Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults@2023-07-01' = {
  name: 'kv-shop-prod'
  properties: {
    tenantId: subscription().tenantId
    sku: { family: 'A', name: 'standard' }
    enableRbacAuthorization: true          // ⭐ RBAC, not the legacy access-policy model
    enableSoftDelete: true                 // on by default and cannot be disabled 🔄
    softDeleteRetentionInDays: 90
    enablePurgeProtection: true            // ⚠️ IRREVERSIBLE once enabled
    publicNetworkAccess: 'Disabled'
    networkAcls: { defaultAction: 'Deny', bypass: 'AzureServices' }
  }
}
Model Verdict
Azure RBAC ⭐ Use this. Consistent with the rest of Azure, supports management groups, PIM, and granular per-secret scope
Access policies (legacy) Vault-wide only, a separate permission model, no PIM. Migrate away

The roles you need:

Role Grants
Key Vault Secrets User ⭐ Read secret values — what your app needs
Key Vault Secrets Officer Manage secrets (create, update, delete) — for pipelines and admins
Key Vault Crypto User Perform key operations
Key Vault Certificates Officer Manage certificates
Key Vault Reader See metadata but not values — useful for auditors
Key Vault Administrator Everything on the data plane

⚠️ Contributor on the vault does NOT grant access to secrets with RBAC authorisation enabled. It's control plane only. This is the single most common Key Vault 403. (Though note: a Contributor can grant themselves the data role, which is why Contributor on production vaults should be rare.)

💡 Scope per-secret where it matters. RBAC supports assignment at the individual secret scope, so a service can read only its own secret rather than everything in the vault.

3. Soft delete and purge protection

Feature Effect
Soft delete A deleted vault or secret is recoverable for the retention period (7–90 days). Always on, cannot be disabled 🔄
Purge protection ⚠️ Deleted objects cannot be permanently purged until retention expires. Irreversible once enabled

⚠️ Two consequences that bite:

  1. The vault name stays reserved during the soft-delete window. Delete kv-shop-dev and try to recreate it → "the vault name is already in use". You must recover or purge it (az keyvault purge) — and with purge protection on, you simply wait.
  2. This breaks ephemeral test environments that create and destroy vaults with the same name. Either use a random suffix, or don't put a vault in the disposable part of your infrastructure.

💡 Enable purge protection in production (it's required for customer-managed keys anyway) and leave it off in dev.

4. Using Key Vault from ASP.NET Core

4.1 Option A: the configuration provider

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

if (!builder.Environment.IsDevelopment())
{
    builder.Configuration.AddAzureKeyVault(
        new Uri($"https://{builder.Configuration["KeyVaultName"]}.vault.azure.net/"),
        new DefaultAzureCredential(),
        new AzureKeyVaultConfigurationOptions
        {
            // ⚠️ Reload is polling-based and costs a listing call each time.
            // Only enable it if you actually need runtime rotation without a restart.
            ReloadInterval = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(30),
        });
}

Naming: Key Vault secret names allow only alphanumerics and hyphens, so -- maps to the configuration separator :.

Secret name:  ConnectionStrings--Default
Config key:   ConnectionStrings:Default
Read as:      builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("Default")

⚠️ Secrets are loaded at startup. Without ReloadInterval, rotating a secret in the vault does nothing until the app restarts.

4.2 Option B ⭐: Key Vault references in App Service configuration

App setting name:  ConnectionStrings__Default
App setting value: @Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=https://kv-shop-prod.vault.azure.net/secrets/SqlConnection/)

The platform resolves the reference with the app's managed identity and injects the plain value as an environment variable. Your code has no Key Vault dependency at all — no SDK, no startup latency, no extra failure mode.

💡 This is the best default for App Service and Functions. Use the configuration provider only when you need programmatic access or you're not on App Service.

⚠️ Omit the version from the SecretUri (.../secrets/SqlConnection/ rather than .../secrets/SqlConnection/abc123) so rotation is picked up when the platform refreshes references 🔄. And check the app-settings blade — a failed reference shows a red status there and usually stops the app from starting.

4.3 Option C: the SDK directly

builder.Services.AddAzureClients(clients =>
{
    clients.AddSecretClient(new Uri(vaultUri));
    clients.UseCredential(new DefaultAzureCredential());
});

public sealed class SigningService(SecretClient secrets, IMemoryCache cache)
{
    public async Task<string> GetApiKeyAsync(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        // ⭐ CACHE. Key Vault is rate-limited and adds ~50–100 ms per call.
        return await cache.GetOrCreateAsync("apikey", async entry =>
        {
            entry.AbsoluteExpirationRelativeToNow = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(30);
            var secret = await secrets.GetSecretAsync("ExternalApiKey", cancellationToken: ct);
            return secret.Value.Value;
        }) ?? throw new InvalidOperationException("Secret not found");
    }
}

⚠️ Never call Key Vault on every request. Vaults have per-vault throttling limits (a few thousand transactions per 10 seconds 🔄); a busy app that fetches a secret per request will get 429s and your latency will include a network round trip every time.

5. Secret rotation

Rotation only works if the application can accept a new value without downtime, which requires designing for two valid secrets during the overlap.

flowchart LR
    A["1. Generate a NEW credential<br/>at the source system"] --> B["2. Store it as a new VERSION<br/>in Key Vault"]
    B --> C["3. Both old and new are valid<br/>at the source (overlap window)"]
    C --> D["4. Applications pick up the new value<br/>(restart / refresh / reference reload)"]
    D --> E["5. Verify nothing is still using the old one"]
    E --> F["6. Revoke the old credential"]

Patterns:

Pattern How
Two-key rotation Services with primary/secondary keys (Storage, Cosmos, Service Bus, Redis): use key1, rotate key2, switch, rotate key1. Never a gap
Event-driven Key Vault emits SecretNearExpiry via Event Grid → a Function rotates it and updates the source system
App Configuration sentinel ⭐ Rotate the secret, then bump a sentinel key; apps watching the sentinel refresh (§7)
Restart-based Simplest: rotate, then restart/swap the app. Fine if you deploy often

💡 The best rotation strategy is not having a secret. Managed identity has nothing to rotate. Rotate only what you genuinely can't federate — third-party API keys, legacy systems.

Set expiry dates on secrets (exp) and alert on SecretNearExpiry events. ⚠️ A silent expiry at 3am on a bank holiday is a real and recurring outage class — especially service principal secrets with a two-year default lifetime that nobody diarised.

6. Certificates

Key Vault manages the full certificate lifecycle: generate/import, auto-renew from an integrated CA (DigiCert, GlobalSign), and notify on expiry.

Integration points:

  • App Service / Application Gateway / Front Door can reference a vault certificate and pick up renewals automatically.
  • The certificate's private key is also stored as a secret — retrieving the secret gives you the PFX, which is how apps load it.
  • ⚠️ Certificate renewal doesn't automatically restart your app. If you load the cert into memory at startup, you keep using the old one until you restart or implement a refresh.

💡 For public TLS on App Service, App Service Managed Certificates are free and auto-renewing — use those unless you need a wildcard or a specific CA.

7. Azure App Configuration

Key Vault is for secrets. App Configuration is for everything else that should change without a redeploy — feature flags, thresholds, endpoints, toggles.

Key Vault App Configuration
For Secrets, keys, certificates Non-secret settings + feature flags
Cost per read Higher, rate-limited Cheap, designed for frequent reads
Dynamic refresh Polling only ⭐ Built-in refresh with a sentinel key
Labels ✘ ⭐ Per-environment values for the same key
Point-in-time restore ✘ ✔
Feature flags ✘ ✔ First class 
builder.Configuration.AddAzureAppConfiguration(options =>
{
    options.Connect(new Uri(appConfigEndpoint), new DefaultAzureCredential())
        // Load values for this environment via LABELS — one store, many environments
        .Select(KeyFilter.Any, LabelFilter.Null)
        .Select(KeyFilter.Any, builder.Environment.EnvironmentName)

        // ⭐ Key Vault references resolved transparently
        .ConfigureKeyVault(kv => kv.SetCredential(new DefaultAzureCredential()))

        // ⭐ The sentinel pattern: poll ONE key; when it changes, reload EVERYTHING.
        // This means one cheap poll instead of polling every key.
        .ConfigureRefresh(refresh => refresh
            .Register("Sentinel", refreshAll: true)
            .SetCacheExpiration(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30)))

        .UseFeatureFlags(ff => ff.SetRefreshInterval(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30)));
});

builder.Services.AddAzureAppConfiguration();
builder.Services.AddFeatureManagement();

var app = builder.Build();
app.UseAzureAppConfiguration();      // ⚠️ required — this middleware triggers the refresh check

Feature flags:

public sealed class RebalanceController(IFeatureManager features) : ControllerBase
{
    [HttpPost]
    public async Task<IActionResult> Rebalance(CancellationToken ct)
    {
        if (await features.IsEnabledAsync("NewRebalanceEngine"))
            return Ok(await _newEngine.RunAsync(ct));

        return Ok(await _legacyEngine.RunAsync(ct));
    }
}

// Declaratively on an endpoint
[FeatureGate("BulkImport")]
[HttpPost("import")]
public async Task<IActionResult> Import(...) { ... }

Filters let you target flags: percentage rollout, time window, or a custom filter (by tenant, user, or region). This is what turns a deploy into a controlled release.

⚠️ Flag debt is real. Every flag is a branch in the code and a combinatorial test case. Set an expiry on each and delete it after full rollout — a codebase with 200 live flags is untestable.

💡 The layered configuration architecture that works:

appsettings.json          → structural defaults, committed
App Configuration         → environment-specific values + feature flags, changeable at runtime
  └─ Key Vault reference  → the secret values, resolved transparently
Environment variables     → per-instance overrides

8. Networking and monitoring

Private endpoint + publicNetworkAccess: Disabled for production vaults, with the privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net DNS zone linked. ⚠️ Same DNS trap as everywhere else — without the zone, the name resolves publicly and times out.

bypass: 'AzureServices' in the network ACLs is usually necessary so App Service Key Vault references and other platform integrations still work.

Logging — enable diagnostic settings to Log Analytics on day one:

// Who accessed which secret, and did it succeed?
AzureDiagnostics
| where ResourceProvider == "MICROSOFT.KEYVAULT"
| where OperationName in ("SecretGet", "SecretList", "KeySign")
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, id_s, identity_claim_appid_g, ResultSignature, CallerIPAddress
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// Failures — a spike usually means a rotation broke something or an identity lost its role
AzureDiagnostics
| where ResourceProvider == "MICROSOFT.KEYVAULT" and ResultSignature != "OK"
| summarize count() by ResultSignature, identity_claim_appid_g, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)

Alert on: 403s (a permission problem or an attack), 429s (you're not caching), and SecretNearExpiry events.

9. Secret hygiene beyond Key Vault

Practice Detail
Detect leaks in CI gitleaks/trufflehog in the pipeline and as a pre-commit hook
On a leak: rotate first The credential is compromised the moment it's pushed. Rewriting history doesn't un-clone it
No secrets in logs Scrub before logging; never log a whole request/response object that might contain one
No secrets in image layers A file deleted in a later layer is still in the image history
No secrets in deployment outputs ⚠️ Bicep/ARM deployment outputs are readable in the deployment history
User secrets for local dev dotnet user-secrets set "ConnectionStrings:Default" "..." — stored outside the repo
Separate secrets per environment Dev credentials must be useless in production 
# Local development — never a .env file in the repo
dotnet user-secrets init
dotnet user-secrets set "ExternalApi:Key" "dev-key-value"

10. Troubleshooting

Error Cause
403 Forbidden on a secret Missing Key Vault Secrets User (Contributor is not enough); or RBAC hasn't propagated; or the vault uses access policies and you granted RBAC (or vice versa)
429 Too Many Requests Not caching — you're fetching per request
Vault name "already in use" when creating Soft-deleted vault holding the name — recover it or az keyvault purge
App Service Key Vault reference shows red Managed identity missing, no role assignment, network ACL blocking, or a bad SecretUri
App works in production, fails in the staging slot The slot has its own managed identity — grant it separately
Secret rotated but the app still uses the old value Loaded at startup with no reload; restart, or use App Configuration refresh
Forbidden from a private endpoint Private DNS zone missing, or bypass: AzureServices not set

🧪

az keyvault secret show --vault-name kv-shop-prod --name SqlConnection --query "value" -o tsv
az role assignment list --scope $(az keyvault show -n kv-shop-prod --query id -o tsv) -o table
az keyvault list-deleted -o table          # find soft-deleted vaults holding a name

11. Checklist

  • enableRbacAuthorization: true; legacy access policies not used
  • Apps granted Key Vault Secrets User (data plane), not just Contributor
  • Every slot's managed identity granted separately
  • Soft delete on (mandatory) with a sensible retention; purge protection on in production
  • Private endpoint + publicNetworkAccess: Disabled + private DNS zone, bypass: AzureServices
  • Secrets accessed via App Service Key Vault references where possible — no SDK dependency
  • Secrets cached in the app if fetched via the SDK (never per request)
  • Expiry dates set on secrets; SecretNearExpiry alerting configured
  • Rotation designed with an overlap window; two-key rotation used where supported
  • Diagnostic logging to Log Analytics; alerts on 403 and 429
  • App Configuration for non-secret settings and feature flags, with the sentinel-key refresh pattern
  • Feature flags have owners and expiry dates
  • Secret scanning in CI and pre-commit; no secrets in logs, images, or deployment outputs
  • Local development uses user secrets, never a committed file

🔍 Questions to test yourself

  • Key Vault vs App Configuration? Secrets vs non-secret settings and feature flags. App Configuration is cheaper to read frequently, supports labels and dynamic refresh, and can hold Key Vault references so you get one configuration surface with secrets resolved transparently.
  • How does an app authenticate to Key Vault without a secret? Managed identity — which is the point: you'd otherwise need a secret to fetch your secrets.
  • Why did my app get 403 after I gave it Contributor? Contributor is control plane; reading a secret needs Key Vault Secrets User on the data plane.
  • How do you rotate a secret with zero downtime? Design for two valid credentials during an overlap: generate the new one, store a new version, let apps pick it up (reference reload, App Configuration sentinel, or restart), verify, then revoke the old one. Two-key services make this trivial.
  • Why can't I recreate a Key Vault with the same name? Soft delete reserves the name for the retention period; recover or purge it — and with purge protection you simply wait.
  • What's the sentinel key pattern? Poll one key cheaply; when it changes, reload the whole configuration — instead of polling every key individually.

Sources: Azure Key Vault configuration provider in ASP.NET Core — Microsoft Learn · Secure secrets management in .NET with Azure Key Vault · Secure secret rotation using Azure Key Vault and .NET · Securing ASP.NET Core secrets with Key Vault via App Configuration
